title: Guru Har Rai's gurpurab

lines: A ROBE HELD CLOSE FOR LIFE.
cards: Sikhs tell a story about a boy walking through a garden in a long, flowing robe. As he passes, the hem catches a flower and snaps its stem. The petals fall.
His grandfather sees it and says something gentle: if you wear a robe like that, you have to carry it carefully.
The boy is said to have held his robe gathered close for the rest of his life, so it would never break a flower again. That boy became the seventh Guru. Today: Har Rai.

teach.b: Guru Har Rai was the grandson of Guru Hargobind, and he succeeded him as the seventh Guru while still young. He made his home at Kiratpur, in the hills of Punjab.
The story of the flower is tradition, not a record, but it fits how Sikhs remember him: a gentle man, careful with living things.
At Kiratpur, he's remembered for gardens: fruit trees, flowers, and medicinal herbs. Tradition says he kept a dispensary there, where medicines were made and given freely to anyone who came.
He also kept the armed horsemen his grandfather had begun, but his years as Guru were largely peaceful.

One story about his medicine reaches all the way to the Mughal court. Tradition tells that Dara Shikoh, a son of the emperor Shah Jahan, fell gravely ill, and the court's physicians couldn't find a remedy.

A rare herb was needed, and it was sent from Guru Har Rai's stores. Dara recovered. The striking part is who got the medicine: a prince of the same ruling house that had executed the Guru's great-grandfather, Guru Arjan.
The healer didn't ask which side the patient was on.
Sikh tradition reads that as the teaching heard all through the Gurus' hymns: the One is in everyone, so care goes to everyone.
His gurpurab is marked with kirtan and langar, and some gurdwaras and families mark it with things he'd recognize: planting trees, tending gardens, or volunteering in clinics.

how: On Guru Har Rai's gurpurab, gurdwaras hold kirtan and langar, and some Sikhs mark it by planting trees, tending gardens or serving in health care, remembering the seventh Guru's gardens and medicine.

games.q: a prince of the house that executed your great-grandfather is dying, and only your herbs can help. what does the story say Guru Har Rai did?
games.why: tradition says the herb was sent and Dara Shikoh recovered: the healer didn't ask which side the patient was on.

practice: If there's a plant near you, bring it some water now, slowly, and watch the soil darken; if not, picture one you love, or a tree you pass each day.
As you water, think of one living thing you could be more careful with, a person, an animal, a place, and gather your robe close, so to speak. If you pray, Waheguru can go in with the water.
